Today they strengthen those drafts.","enduringUnderstanding":"Stories from many cultures can teach shared lessons, and clear, carefully revised writing helps a reader see those connections.","futureLessons":"In Lesson 40, students finalize their essays and prepare for the seminar or podcast. Today you become your own editor and a partner's editor. Strong writers rarely get it right in one draft. They revise."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Turn to a partner. Why might a writer reread an essay about shared lessons in myths after finishing it?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Because you might notice places where the idea is confusing or where you forgot to say which myth your evidence came from. It can be removed and the sentence still works. We call it a nonrestrictive element and set it off with commas, parentheses, or dashes. Proper nouns, such as myth titles and cultural groups, need capital letters. Display: the greek myth of perseus which the ancient Greeks told for centuries shows that heroes needs help from others."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What needs to be fixed in this sentence? Look for capitals, commas, and agreement."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Greek and Perseus need capital letters. The Greek myth should start with a capital The. The part 'which the ancient Greeks told for centuries' is extra, so it needs commas around it. 'Heroes needs' should be 'heroes need' because heroes is plural."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"Corrected sentence: The Greek myth of Perseus, which the ancient Greeks told for centuries, shows that heroes need help from others. Note that capitalization applies to Greek because it names a cultural group, and the words myth and heroes stay lowercase. Myth titles such as The Lightning Thief are capitalized and italicized or underlined."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Subject-verb agreement gets tricky in long sentences because words come between the subject and the verb. Find the subject first, cross out the extra phrase, and check the verb."},{"type":"directions","text":"Choose one paragraph in your own draft. Find at least one sentence with an extra element and check its punctuation. Circle every proper noun to confirm the capital letter. Underline one long sentence's subject and verb to check agreement. Do not correct for students. The lightning thief and the greek myths both has heroes. That is what my essay was about.' Think aloud: This conclusion only repeats. The rubric asks me to synthesize ideas across myths, so I should say what the myths teach together and why that matters. Revised: 'Together, The Lightning Thief and the Greek myths of Perseus and Theseus (both stories of young heroes) show that courage grows when characters accept help from others. Readers in every culture can learn from that shared lesson.' Then I edit: capitalize Greek, italicize the title, punctuate the parenthetical, and check that 'show' agrees with its plural subject."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What changed between the first and revised conclusion, and why is the second stronger?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The first one just repeated that the myths have heroes. It also fixed the capitals and the verb and used a formal tone."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Students listen actively to a think-aloud and learn language for describing revisions, while noticing how noun phrases can be expanded to add precision.","sayAsk":"Say: 'I changed ___ to ___ because ___.' Ask: 'What did the writer add to make the conclusion stronger?' Frames: 'The revised sentence is stronger because ___.' 'A noun phrase I could expand is ___, as in ___ (for example, young heroes who accept help).' Let Emerging students point to the changed words and say them aloud with a partner.","watchFor":"If students only say 'it sounds better,' then prompt: 'Which rubric row did the change help, evidence, style, or conclusion?' If students cannot find a change, then underline the old and new phrases together. Does it synthesize ideas across myths, or does it only repeat your thesis? Rewrite it so it names the shared lesson and why it matters. Then use the revision checklist and rubric to revise one more part of your essay for clarity, transitions, or formal style. Finally, edit one paragraph for capitalization, punctuation, spelling, and agreement."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What sentence did you add or change in your conclusion to bring the myths together?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"I changed my last sentence to say that both the myth of Theseus and The Lightning Thief show that being brave means trusting your friends. Before, I only said the stories were alike."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Confer with two or three students whose conclusions only restate the thesis. Frames: 'Together, ___ and ___ show that ___.' 'This lesson matters because ___.' 'Both myths teach that ___.' Encourage students to expand a noun with an adjective, such as courageous heroes or ancient stories.","watchFor":"If students write a conclusion with slang or contractions, then prompt: 'Replace the casual words with precise ones.' If sentences are very short, then prompt: 'Add a describing phrase to a noun.' 'You could strengthen your evidence by ___.' 'One place to make the style more formal is ___.' Also circle one possible convention error and ask the writer to check it. Switch roles and then use the feedback to revise."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What specific feedback did your partner give that you can use to improve your essay?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"My partner said my evidence from the myth of Perseus was not explained. She told me to add a sentence saying how it proves my point. I will add that and fix a capital I missed."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Model one round of feedback with a volunteer before partners begin. Remind students that feedback names a specific spot in the text and ties to the rubric. Reviewers suggest; writers decide."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Students listen actively to a partner's essay and ask and answer questions to give useful feedback.","sayAsk":"Say: 'Read aloud one paragraph while your partner listens.'
